items.title: Tandjouaré : Les capacités des leaders communautaires renforcées pour lutter contre les rumeurs
items.description: Tandjouaré, 19 nov. (ATOP) – Des leaders communautaires, notamment des chefs religieux et traditionnels, des femmes médiatrices et des acteurs de la paix, ont pris part, le mercredi 18 novembre à Tandjouaré, à un agora communautaire consacré à la lutte contre les rumeurs et la désinformation. Cette rencontre est organisée par le Réseau ouest-africain pour l’édification de la paix au Togo (WANEP-Togo). Elle s’intègre dans le cadre de la deuxième phase du projet « Renforcement de la résilience et de l’engagement des communautés pour prévenir et répondre à l’extrémisme violent dans les pays du corridor atlantique ». Placée sous le thème « La rumeur en procès », l’initiative bénéficie de l’appui financier du Programme des Nations unies pour le développement (PNUD). Elle vise à outiller les leaders locaux sur les mécanismes d’identification, d’analyse et de vérification des informations. Les participants ont été amenés à réfléchir aux rumeurs qui circulent dans leurs communautés et aux moyens de prévenir leur propagation. A travers un procès fictif, au cours duquel chacun a joué un rôle précis (juge, témoins, victimes et acteurs communautaires), ils ont mis en scène une situation de rumeur afin d’en comprendre les conséquences sur la cohésion sociale. Les échanges ont également porté sur la vérification des informations, les mécanismes d’alerte et le recours aux sources fiables. Ils ont abouti à l’élaboration de messages de sensibilisation contre la désinformation et les discours de haine, ainsi qu’à des engagements collectifs en faveur de la paix, de la tolérance et du vivre-ensemble. L’animatrice, Mme Lalle Tani, directrice exécutive de l’Association genre des médias des Savanes (GEME-SA), a souligné l’importance de l’implication des acteurs communautaires dans la lutte contre la propagation des rumeurs et des fausses informations. Cette démarche, dit-elle, vise à susciter des engagements individuels et collectifs afin d’éviter le relai de fausses informations et de contribuer à préserver la paix et la cohésion sociale. L’imam de la mosquée de Goundoga, Laré Souleymane, a insisté sur la nécessité de vérifier toute information avant sa diffusion. « Cette formation nous dote de connaissances et d’outils pratiques pour mieux vérifier les informations et freiner la propagation des fausses rumeurs », a-t-il indiqué. ATOP/SYI/JK/BA

items.title: Des tracteurs de forte puissance Belarus bientôt assemblés en Algérie
items.description: L’Algérie compte sur la Biélorussie pour accélérer la mécanisation de son agriculture. En visite à Minsk, le ministre de l'Agriculture Sid Ali Khaldi est revenu à Alger avec dans ses bagages des « projets concrets » qui devraient, en principe, contribuer à réduire les insuffisances du secteur agricole algérien en termes de mécanisation. Deux accords dans le domaine de la machinerie agricole et un accord pour la production du lait infantile en Algérie. C’est là le bilan de la 2e session de la Commission mixte algéro-bélarusse de coopération commerciale, économique, scientifique et technique, tenue le 18 novembre à Minsk, co-présidée par le ministre de l’Agriculture Sid Ali Khaldi et le ministre biélorusse de la Réglementation antimonopole et du Commerce, Aleksandr Vladimirovitch Yakovchits. « Nous sommes passés du stade des intentions et des engagements à celui de la concrétisation effective et opérationnelle de projets réels et concrets, et ce, à travers la signature de 3 accords stratégiques dans des secteurs prioritaires », a déclaré M. Khaldi devant les journalistes. Le premier accord, signé entre l’ETRAG (entreprise publique des tracteurs agricoles) et l’usine de Minsk de tracteurs, porte sur le montage de tracteurs de forte puissance de la marque Belarus, avec intégration progressive de ses composants en Algérie. Le deuxième accord, signé par Sampo Algérie et Gomselmesh, concerne « l’étude de développement et la production de moissonneuses-batteuses automotrices adaptées aux terrains difficiles ». Une usine de lait infantile biélorusse en Algérie Le groupe public Giplait et Bellakt ont signé, de leur côté, un nouveau document qui fera avancer leur partenariat entamé après la signature d’un protocole d’accord, le 16 septembre dernier à Alger. L’accord prévoit la réalisation d’une usine de production de lait infantile en Algérie et l’élaboration du plan d'action de la future joint-venture. Le ministre Khaldi a affirmé que « ces contrats répondent à des priorités nationales : consolider la sécurité alimentaire, implantation de l’industrie, augmentation du taux d’intégration locale, la formation et le transfert des technologies, développer la sous-traitance, création de postes d’emplois et réduction de la facture d’importation ». En attendant la concrétisation de ces projets, les carences en matière de mécanisation constituent l’un des principaux freins au développement de l’activité agricole en Algérie. Des agriculteurs qui ont investi de l’argent et consenti de grands efforts se trouvent parfois dans l’incapacité de récolter le fruit de leur labeur, faute de moissonneuses-batteuses . Pendant la campagne de récolte des céréales 2026, ces machines ont cruellement manqué. Et à travers les vastes plaines du pays, il n’est pas rare de voir des agriculteurs arracher la pomme de terre avec des outils traditionnels et en mobilisant une main-d’œuvre nombreuse et mal payée. Ces insuffisances ont un impact direct sur les rendements de l’activité agricole. Et la grande majorité des agriculteurs n’a pas les moyens de s’équiper correctement malgré les aides fournies par l’État aux agriculteurs pour l’acquisition du matériel agricole, à travers des aides directes ou des crédits bonifiés. À titre d’exemple, une moissonneuse-batteuse fabriquée localement par Sampo Algérie coûte entre 9,8 et 12 millions de dinars. Un tracteur Massey-Fergusson (150 chevaux) assemblé à Oued Hamimine, dans la wilaya de Constantine, peut coûter jusqu’à 8,5 millions de dinars. L’article Des tracteurs de forte puissance Belarus bientôt assemblés en Algérie est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Debate electoral 29-N, en directo | Sánchez y Feijóo llegan para el cara a cara y apuran los últimos minutos para prepararse con sus equipos
items.description: Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo ya están en el estudio de Madrid Content City, donde a partir de las 22.00 se miden en su único debate antes de las elecciones generales del 29-N. Feijóo ha llegado sobre un cuarto de hora antes que Sánchez, en un orden que se ha decidido por sorteo, igual que quién dice la última palabra en cada bloque y de qué lado de la mesa se sienta cada uno. Los dos candidatos están acompañados por sus asesores hasta que empiece el debate. Durante las dos pausas publicitarias, de tres minutos cada una, los asesores podrán volver a entrar en el plató, pero sin dispositivos electrónicos. Sánchez ha preparado el cara a cara con su núcleo duro en La Moncloa y con la “lección aprendida” de 2023, cuando casi todos los análisis dieron por ganador a Feijóo. El líder del PP lo ha preparado con su equipo de confianza procedente de la Xunta de Galicia, esta vez sin Miguel Ángel Rodríguez, jefe de gabinete de Isabel Díaz Ayuso. En el PP dicen que irá “a la yugular”, aunque tratando de no arriesgar su perfil presidencial. El debate, organizado por la Academia de la Televisión y moderado por su presidenta, María Casado, dura 90 minutos y se divide en cinco bloques temáticos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Africa’s ‘basic’ payments tier swells to 19 as Liberia, five others join AfricaNenda ranking
items.description: The number of African instant payment systems rated at the entry level of a continental inclusion ranking rose to 19 this year from 15, as new systems in Liberia, Burundi and Guinea went live and three existing rails added merchant payments, according to a report launched on Thursday. The basic tier, which now spans 14 countries, grew faster than any other level in the AfricaNenda Foundation’s fifth State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems in Africa (SIIPS) report, published in partnership with the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa and the World Bank Group. The number of systems that do not qualify for any level fell to eight from 10. Eleven systems are rated progressed, up from 10 after the West African Economic and Monetary Union’s PI-SPI entered at that level, and Nigeria’s NIBSS Instant Payment remains the only system in Africa rated mature. To qualify as basic, a system must support the channel most people use in its market and must handle both person-to-person and merchant payments, under the report’s criteria. Three systems that already existed made the cut this year. Kenya’s PesaLink, Sierra Leone’s Salone Payment Switch (SaPS) and the Southern African Development Community’s Transactions Cleared on an Immediate Basis (TCIB) system “moved from not ranked to basic after adding support for the P2B use case,” the report said. P2B refers to payments from people to businesses, such as a customer paying a shopkeeper. Three national systems that went live during the year entered the ranking at the same level: Pay Na-Na in Liberia, BurundiPay in Burundi and NimbaPay in Guinea. The tier’s net gain was four because two mobile money systems in Tanzania and Nigeria were folded into their countries’ main rails. Of the 36 systems assessed in both 2025 and 2026, three moved up a tier and the rest held their positions, “reinforcing the trend of gradual progress toward broader inclusion,” the report said. But it also found that “the number of systems is increasing in parallel with, yet faster than, improvements in system inclusivity.” THE NEWCOMERS LIBERIA. Pay Na-Na went live on December 16, 2025, linking the country’s two mobile money operators, Lone Star MTN and Orange Liberia. The report said it is classified as basic because it “only had mobile money providers as participants by the end of the research period.” Central Bank of Liberia Executive Governor Henry F. Saamoi told JoyNews in an interview on Wednesday, a day before the launch, that banks were the next target. “All of the commercial banks work in silo. They are not interoperable,” he said. He said a National Electronic Payment Switch, built on the Pay Na-Na platform and due in the first quarter of 2027, would “onboard them to make them interoperable.” “So in the comfort of your bed you are able to do transaction from bank A to bank B. Today that doesn’t work,” he said. The central bank says Pay Na-Na was delivered in 73 business days. Saamoi said he had been told no other country had moved as fast, and that others could learn from how quickly Liberia built the system “in a country that has been deprived of interoperability.” Civil servants are now “able to receive their payments, their salary payments in real time without any deductions,” he said. Liberia’s financial inclusion rate stands at 52%, and the central bank wants to reach 75% by the end of 2029. “The IPS is the gateway for you to achieve that because it helps you to bring people from the informal sector into the formal sector,” Saamoi said. BURUNDI. The Bank of the Republic of Burundi launched BurundiPay on April 23, 2026. The central bank wholly owns and operates the system, which supports person-to-person, person-to-business, business-to-person and business-to-business payments. Regulation issued at launch requires all financial institutions in the country to join by September 2026. Four commercial banks, nine microfinance institutions and one mobile money operator, Cashtel, had done so by July 31, the report said. GUINEA. The Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea launched NimbaPay on July 22, 2026. Implemented by Guinéenne de Monétique on Mojaloop, the same open-source platform as Pay Na-Na, it allowed person-to-person payments at launch, with payments to government and cross-border transfers planned for later phases. THE MOVERS KENYA. PesaLink, run by Integrated Payment Systems Ltd (IPSL), opened its payment rails to third-party developers in October 2025 through a fintech programme, the report said. It placed PesaLink among systems “which are otherwise close to achieving progressed status,” but said non-bank participants do not appear to be represented in its governance and that the Central Bank of Kenya has “no direct involvement in scheme-level governance.” SIERRA LEONE. The Bank of Sierra Leone launched its National Payment Switch in May 2023 and directed all commercial banks and mobile money operators to route domestic instant payments through SaPS from April 1, 2025. The report lists SaPS among the systems that still lack pro-poor governance or central bank involvement. SOUTHERN AFRICA. TCIB, one of four regional instant payment systems on the continent, enables cross-border payments across Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe, according to the report, which also lists it among the systems with governance gaps. A CEILING FOR SOME “For basic systems, a structural cap persists,” the report said. Nine of the basic systems serve only banks or only mobile money providers and do not connect to a cross-domain system, so they cannot meet the interoperability test needed to reach the progressed level. Of the eight domestic cross-domain systems at the basic level, some, including Pay Na-Na and Algeria’s Switch Mobile, do not yet allow all payment service providers to take part. Others, including PesaLink and SaPS, lack pro-poor governance or central bank involvement. Even for systems already at the progressed level, the report expects few to go further. “Further advancement past the progressed level will likely remain the exception,” it said, until systems broaden the uses they support, strengthen ways for users to resolve problems and bring in more participants

items.title: Justice en France : le siège du Rassemblement national à nouveau perquisitionné
items.description: En France, l'inspection generale de la police nationale (IGPN), a perquisitionne le siege du Rassemblement national, a rapporte ce 19 novembre le quotidien Le Monde , precisant qu'une information judiciaire a ete ouverte fin juillet par le parquet de Paris, pour « violation du secret professionnel », « violation du secret de l'enquete » et « recel » de ces delits. La perquisition du siege de ce parti, dont la candidate est la grande favorite de la prochaine election presidentielle, aurait eu lieu le 9 novembre. Par ailleurs, toujours selon la meme source, le ministere de l'Interieur a egalement ete perquisitionne « fin octobre ». Des perquisitions confirmees aupres de l'AFP par la Place Beauvau – concernant celle du ministere - et par le parquet concernant celle du siege du parti a la flamme. Le haut fonctionnaire soupconne est l'ancien secretaire general du ministere, Hugues Moutouh, actuellement prefet du Loiret et de la region Centre-Val de Loire, a aussi precise une source proche du dossier. Sollicite, le parquet de Paris a indique avoir « ouvert le 27 juillet 2026 une information judiciaire portant sur des faits de violation du secret professionnel, violation du secret de l'enquete et recel de ces delits ». Cette procedure dite « incidente » ferait suite aux investigations menees par l'office central de lutte contre la corruption et les infractions financieres et fiscales, dans le cadre de l'enquete ouverte en juillet 2025 par le Parquet europeen sur l'usage des fonds alloues au groupe Identite et democratie (ID) au Parlement europeen ou les eurodeputes RN ont siege entre 2019 et 2024. « Les perquisitions ont fait emerger des elements, laissant penser que le RN beneficiait d'informations confidentielles sur des enquetes judiciaires visant le parti en provenance d'au moins un cadre du ministere de l'Interieur », a rapporte Le Monde , sans nommer ce haut fonctionnaire « qui a depuis change d'affectation ». Selon l'AFP, qui cite une source proche du dossier, il s'agirait du prefet du Loiret et de la region Centre-Val de Loire, Hugues Moutouh.

items.title: Deputy Interior Minister urges REGSECs to adopt proactive security management
items.description: Deputy Interior Minister Ebenezer Okletey Terlabi has urged Regional Security Councils (REGSECs) and local government authorities in the Bono, Bono East and Ahafo Regions to adopt proactive approaches to security management to prevent emerging threats from escalating. He said effective security management requires preventive action, responsible leadership and early intervention in potential conflicts, rather than waiting for incidents to occur before responding. Mr Terlabi made the call at a workshop on the Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168), for REGSEC members and Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) from the three regions in Sunyani. The Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168), modernises Ghana’s national security and intelligence governance framework. Enacted in March 2026, it replaces the Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2020 (Act 1030). The Deputy Minister stressed that security was critical to development and the creation of an environment where people could pursue their livelihoods without fear. He noted that the Bono, Bono East and Ahafo Regions had considerable potential in agriculture, commerce and natural resources, but said such opportunities could not be fully realised in an atmosphere of unresolved disputes, criminal activity and insecurity. He said the workshop was expected to deepen participants’ understanding of Act 1168, clarify their respective security responsibilities and strengthen collaboration among the three regions. Mr Terlabi urged participants to ensure that the knowledge acquired translated into practical action in managing security concerns within their jurisdictions. He further called on them to strengthen their respective Regional Security Councils and establish effective communication channels with security agencies, warning against waiting until crises emerge before seeking intervention. The Deputy Minister said early engagement, coordination and preventive measures were essential to addressing security challenges and maintaining peace across the regions.

items.title: My Day, My Rights, My Future
items.description: Have you ever woken up and wondered what a child’s day looks like? Have you paused to imagine what goes through their minds, the dreams they have, and the challenges they face? Perhaps we see children every day, but how often do we take time to understand the world through their eyes? For some children, a day is filled with laughter, learning, friendship, and love from parents and significant others. Yet for many more, it comes with hunger, fear, neglect, and uncertainty. Sometimes, we take these little things for granted, forgetting that a safe home, quality education, a listening ear, and the freedom to play can mean everything to a child. Today, as we mark World Children’s Day 2026, let us reflect on some important questions: are we doing enough to give every child the childhood they deserve? How is the day of an child? Are their rights being protected? Are their voices heard? and How secured is their future? In Ghana, the everyday life of a child is nothing ordinary; it is a roller-coaster of events — from performing academic duties such as studying, to activities such as performing chores, playing, or basically just having fun. These moments may seem small and mundane, but they are not. They reflect whether a child’s access to education, right to identity, protection, health, and participation in decisions that affect their lives are being fulfilled. One of the basic ways we can actualise these rights is presenting children with the right to identity. Birth registration is the very first affirmation of the identity a child holds. A child born in Ghana, to Ghanaian parents is considered Ghanaian and, therefore, should be recognised as such. Birth registration in my opinion gives the child a legal identity and citizenship. Yet, in many rural communities and busy towns across the country, countless children grow up without this vital document simply because their parents could not easily access a Births and Deaths Registry after delivery. Years later, when that same child is ready, for instance, to acquire a Ghana Card, or securing a scholarship, the absence of a birth certificate becomes a hindrance to such opportunities. A child who is not given the opportunity to go through a birth registration process is being deprived of his or her right to identity as a citizen of Ghana. I, therefore, urge parents, guardians, and stakeholders to ensure that every child is registered since it forms part of their fundamental human rights as children. Another crucial right of children that cannot be overlooked is the right to education. As the saying goes, “Education is the key to success”— will denying a child the right to education not be depriving him or her from being successful in the future? Article 25, Clause 1 of the 1992 Constitution of Ghana states that “All persons shall have the right to equal educational opportunities and facilities.” “All persons” means it includes children. However, as an avid reader of the Junior Graphic, I’ve read and seen photos of children, in the bustling streets and the lorry stations in the country during school hours, hawking sachet water, plantain chips, and other wares to support their families, while others in remote communities study under trees due to lack of classroom blocks, while those who are fortunate to study in classrooms also lack furniture, textbooks and qualified teachers. It is our collective responsibility to ensure that every child of school-going age is provided with facilities in order to build a solid foundation for their future. Decision-makers, politicians, parents, community leaders, and most importantly, the government must invest in the education sector to provide quality education for children. These sayings, “The success of a child is the success of the whole nation,” and “The efforts of a country contribute to the success of a child” stipulate that children are the future of every country and government must ensure that polices are put in place to enable them realise their full potentials to achieve Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4. Violence against children is another critical issue that affects children not only in Ghana, but around the globe. Article 28, Clause 3 of the 1992 Constitution of Ghana also states that “A child shall not be subjected to torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.” My understanding of this statement basically is that, under no circumstance should a child be exposed to torture, child labour, sexual and physical abuse. Sadly, in our communities, we still witness young children being subjected to harsh corporal punishment, tedious tasks, domestic and sexual abuse. The Wednesday, November 4-10, 2026, edition of the Junior Graphic, reported that over 53,000 teen girls got pregnant in just seven months and violence against girls and lack of sex education were the major causes. Children are supposed to be nurtured with absolute care and love, not only by parents and guardians, but from the people around them. The love and care shown to us children help in the development of our mental and psychological well-being. Moreover, children should be given the opportunity to share their opinions on matters that affect them. In many homes and schools, the old adage that “children should be seen and not heard” still silences young people, even when decisions are being made about their schooling, welfare, and future. Yet, when we are given platforms such as the Junior Graphic, school clubs, community durbars, or children’s parliaments to express ourselves, we offer honest solutions to the everyday challenges we face. These opportunities are like voices given to children to speak up and talk about their problems. We are given the opportunity to own our future by making decisions and sharing opinions. Media platforms, community leaders, parents, and guardians can come together to turn children’s voices into public action. I Princess Enam Avoxe, the Winner of the 2025 Junior Graphic National Essay Competition organised by the Graphic Communication Group Ltd, strongly urge the Government of Ghana, stakeholders, and the world at large to put in efforts to ensure the rights of children are protected and their voices heard. For a child saved today is a future generation secured. Princess Enam, Avoxe 2025 Junior Graphic Essay Competition Winner, Sonrise Christian High School, Ho.

items.title: Engineers must stop ‘pocket building’ to prevent building collapses – Ahmed Ibrahim
items.description: The Minister for Works, Housing and Water Resources, Ahmed Ibrahim, has urged engineers to uphold professional standards and resist practices that compromise the quality and safety of buildings, warning that “pocket building” could contribute to building collapses. He said engineers must ensure that construction projects are executed according to approved designs, specifications and professional standards, rather than the financial limitations or preferences of clients. Speaking at the Institution of Engineering and Technology Ghana (IET-GH) 40th Annual General Conference and Induction Ceremony on Thursday, November 19, the Minister criticised situations where building owners dictate the quantity and quality of materials to be used, resulting in structures being built below required standards. He described the practice as “pocket engineering”, where contractors and artisans adjust construction work to suit the money available to clients instead of following the specifications required for safe construction. “Integrity, accountability, diligence and adherence to professional standards must remain non-negotiable values within the profession. Unlike Ghana, where we do pocket building or pocket engineering,” he said. Mr Ibrahim explained that some building owners often instruct workers to use fewer construction materials than required, a practice he said undermines the professional training and judgement of engineers. He questioned why engineers would allow clients to determine the quantity of materials needed for construction when they had been trained to establish the appropriate specifications. “When the owner of the house tells you that you need 10 bags of cement, but he has only three, and you say you can do it with three, you are building according to my pocket, not according to the professional standards you were taught,” he said. He warned that such compromises could have serious consequences for public safety, particularly when construction standards were ignored. “Why wouldn’t houses collapse? Why wouldn’t buildings collapse when standards are compromised?” he asked. The Minister called on engineers to take responsibility for ensuring that construction work met the required standards, regardless of pressure from clients or project owners. Mr Ibrahim also urged engineers to take a leading role in the execution of infrastructure projects and ensure that contracts were awarded to competent professionals and companies with the capacity to deliver. Drawing on his experience as a former Minister for Local Government, he said political interference and the award of contracts to contractors without the necessary capacity had contributed to delays and the failure of some government projects. He cited his experience in implementing the 24-hour economy markets initiative, explaining that he had sought advice from colleagues on how to avoid challenges that had affected previous government projects. He said he was advised to avoid political considerations in awarding contracts and to prioritise contractors with the technical and financial capacity to complete projects. Mr Ibrahim said he subsequently adopted a policy of not paying mobilisation fees upfront to contractors under the initiative, insisting that payments would be made based on work completed. “If you lay the foundation, we will pay you. If you don’t go to the site, we will cancel it and give it to a new contractor,” he said. He urged engineers to ensure that engineering and construction companies were established and managed by people with the necessary technical expertise, rather than allowing business interests alone to determine how projects were executed. The Minister described engineers as key contributors to national development, saying their expertise translates government policies and development plans into infrastructure and services that improve people’s lives. He said engineers and technicians played critical roles in the planning, design, construction, operation and maintenance of infrastructure across several sectors, including housing, water, transport, energy, telecommunications, agriculture and manufacturing. In the water sector, he said engineers were helping to expand access to safe and reliable water, rehabilitate ageing infrastructure and introduce technologies to improve efficiency. In housing, he said their expertise was essential to addressing the growing demand for affordable and quality housing through modern construction methods, innovative building materials and efficient project delivery. He added that engineers were also needed to develop resilient infrastructure capable of supporting economic growth while withstanding climate change and environmental pressures. Mr Ibrahim urged engineers to take greater responsibility in public sector development, arguing that their technical expertise should be given more prominence in decision-making at the local and national levels. He said Ghana needed a strong pool of trained and professional engineers to support its development ambitions.

items.title: CRIEF : des 20 milliards de la LONAGUI au « Nabayagate », Charles Wright apporte des précisions
items.description: Screenshot " data-large-file="https://i0.wp.com/mediaguinee.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/IMG_1894.jpeg?fit=1024%2C691&ssl=1" /> Deux dossiers, deux enjeux judiciaires qui retiennent l'attention. Sur le plateau de Télé 24, le procureur spécial près la CRIEF (Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières), Alphonse Charles Wright, s'est exprimé sur le reversement de 20 milliards de francs guinéens par la LONAGUI au Trésor public et sur les développements de l'affaire Nabayagate. Entre récupération des fonds de l'État et soupçons de corruption autour des accusations visant Zénab Nabaya Dramé, le magistrat a tenu à préciser la position de son parquet. Le premier concerne les 20 milliards de francs guinéens déjà reversés au Trésor public par la LONAGUI. Une somme que le magistrat présente comme une première étape dans une procédure visant à obtenir la restitution de ressources publiques qui, selon lui, auraient été conservées pendant plusieurs années sans justification légale. À en croire le procureur spécial, les redevances dues à l'État auraient été retenues pendant deux à trois ans par la société. « Vous avez une structure de jeu qui exploite et qui devrait, en principe sans qu'on ne l'oblige, à s'acquitter des redevances de l'État. Mais ça fait presque deux à trois ans que ces montants-là sont retenus par devers eux. Il y a une forme de tentative de détournement des deniers publics », a-t-il expliqué. Pour Alphonse Charles Wright, il ne s'agit pas simplement d'un problème de paiement de redevances, mais d'une question susceptible de relever de la répression des infractions économiques et financières. « Nous ne sommes pas dans le cas de recouvrement d'impôts ou de redevances. Nous sommes dans le cas de faire réprimer en principe une tentative de détournement des deniers publics », a-t-il insisté. Le directeur général de la LONAGUI aurait pris l'engagement de reverser le reste des sommes réclamées dans un délai de dix jours. Mais le procureur spécial ne semble pas disposé à attendre nécessairement jusqu'à l'expiration de cette échéance. « Le directeur s'est engagé d'ailleurs. Je serai obligé d'abréger ce délai de 10 jours. Parce que pour moi, l'argent-là, ce qui ça a été déplacé utilisé à d'autres fins, il faut qu'on ramène maintenant-là », a-t-il prévenu. Au cours de cet entretien, le procureur spécial a également expliqué l'approche qu'il entend désormais privilégier dans le traitement des dossiers économiques et financiers. Selon lui, l'incarcération ne doit pas être systématique lorsque les personnes mises en cause manifestent une volonté réelle de restituer les ressources publiques. « Notre politique pénale a changé. On ne va pas continuer à envoyer les gens en prison. Nous estimons aujourd'hui […] ça ne sert à rien d'envoyer les gens en prison si ils ont la volonté et la bonne foi de redonner à l'État son dû », a-t-il déclaré. Il prévient toutefois que cette orientation ne signifie pas une tolérance envers les pratiques portant atteinte aux finances publiques. D'autres structures, notamment des établissements publics administratifs et des sociétés redevables de dividendes à l'État, pourraient également être concernées. L'autre temps fort de cette intervention concerne l'affaire Nabayagate, liée aux accusations de détournement de fonds visant l'ancienne ministre Zénab Nabaya. Interrogé sur la décision de non-lieu concernant cette dernière et sur la situation de Youssouf Boundou Sylla, le procureur spécial a tenu à distinguer les éventuelles poursuites pour diffamation des faits qui relèveraient de la compétence de la CRIEF. Pour Alphonse Charles Wright, la question centrale concernant Boundou n'est pas uniquement celle des accusations formulées contre l'ancienne ministre, mais celle des éventuelles sommes d'argent qu'il aurait reçues dans ce contexte. « Monsieur Boundou va être poursuivi pas parce qu'il a diffamé, ça c'est pas un problème, ça c'est les lois du droit commun. Si la victime estime qu'elle peut porter son action devant les tribunaux de droit commun, elle peut le faire. Mais moi en tant que procureur spécial, compétent dans le cadre de la répression des infractions relavant de nos attributions, monsieur Boundou a écrit, il a reçu combien de montants ? Au fait, le problème pour moi, c'est là », a-t-il précisé. Le magistrat évoque ainsi des soupçons de corruption qui, selon lui, méritent d'être examinés par la justice. « S'il a donné l'argent, il y a une pratique présumée de corruption qui s'installe là. C'est de cela il s'agit », a-t-il ajouté. Le procureur spécial estime que les éventuelles questions de diffamation peuvent être examinées par les juridictions compétentes de droit commun. Son intérêt, dans le cadre de ses attributions, porte plutôt sur l'existence présumée d'une contrepartie financière. « Nous ne tolérerons aucun manque de respect à l'institution judiciaire » Au-delà du dossier Boundou, Alphonse Charles Wright a également réagi aux prises de position de certains acteurs, notamment dans le milieu de la presse. S'il reconnaît le droit des journalistes à défendre leurs confrères, il estime que cela ne doit pas conduire à remettre en cause le respect dû à l'institution judiciaire. Il a notamment évoqué le cas du journaliste Lansana Camara, affirmant que celui-ci avait reconnu avoir rédigé un texte sur la base d'indications reçues dans un bar-café, avant de porter de graves accusations contre un ancien ministre des Affaires étrangères. Pour le procureur spécial, les accusations visant des responsables publics peuvent avoir des répercussions sur l'image du pays. Il a donc tenu à adresser un avertissement à ceux qui contestent les procédures judiciaires en cours. « Donc je suis pas là à répondre à qui que ce soit, mais nous ne tolérerons pas dans tous les cas aucun manque de respect à l'institution judiciaire. Bien. Pour nous, c'est la ligne rouge », a-t-il conclu. Christine Finda Kamano L’article CRIEF : des 20 milliards de la LONAGUI au « Nabayagate », Charles Wright apporte des précisions est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Road construction diversion linked to fresh crash at Kasoa- Winneba Highway
items.description: The traffic diversion created by ongoing road construction on the Kasoa–Winneba Highway has come under scrutiny following a crash at Gomoa Potsin Junction that left several passengers, including students, injured. The accident involved a Benz Sprinter with registration number GW 2208-25, which was travelling from Kasoa towards Potsin. According to reports, the driver was travelling at high speed when he attempted to swerve to avoid a taxi making a U-turn at the intersection. He reportedly lost control of the vehicle in the process, causing both front tyres to burst and leaving several passengers injured Those seated at the front of the Sprinter are said to have sustained particularly serious injuries, while the driver was also severely injured. Most of the injured passengers were students travelling to school, including students from Apam Senior High School, Cape Coast Senior High School and Aggrey Memorial A.M.E. Zion Senior High School. The victims were rushed to the Potsin Polyclinic for medical attention. No deaths have been reported in connection with the accident. The vehicles involved have since been towed from the scene to allow traffic to flow along the highway. Although several people sustained injuries, no deaths have been reported in connection with the accident. The vehicles involved have since been towed from the accident scene to facilitate the free flow of traffic along the highway.

items.title: The Law 101: Arrested? Detained? Denied Bail? Know Your Rights! (AG Ayine’s new directive and what it means for you)
items.description: Today, Thursday, 19 th November 2026, I bring you another edition of THE LAW 101 , my public legal education series. For years, we have complained about arbitrary arrests, unlawful detention, coerced confessions, demands for money before bail, the humiliation of suspects and the misuse of criminal investigations to settle personal scores. I have hosted countless editions of my weekly legal clinic, THE LAW , educating the public on these matters. I have lost count of the number of times I have devoted Samson’s Take to these abuses, granted interviews or published articles and social media posts drawing attention to them. Yet the abuses persist. But what do our laws actually say about these practices? And what should you know if the police or another law-enforcement agency arrests or investigates you? On 2 nd November 2026, Attorney-General and Minister for Justice, Dr Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, issued a comprehensive directive on constitutional and legal compliance in criminal investigations. It is an important intervention, not because it creates entirely new rights, but because it reminds investigators of their existing legal obligations and demands compliance. Here are ten things you should know. 1. THE POLICE CANNOT ARREST YOU JUST BECAUSE SOMEONE HAS COMPLAINED ABOUT YOU. An arrest must have a lawful basis. Under Article 14 of the Constitution and the Criminal and Other Offences (Procedure) Act, 1960, Act 30, police officers must have the legal authority and requisite grounds to arrest. A complaint does not automatically justify an arrest. And the police must not use criminal investigations to enforce contracts, recover debts or settle private disputes. A police station is not a debt collection agency! 2. YOU HAVE A RIGHT TO KNOW WHY YOU ARE BEING ARRESTED. Article 14(2) of the Constitution requires that a person arrested, restricted or detained be informed immediately, in a language they understand, of the reasons and their right to a lawyer of their choice. An officer cannot simply arrest you and refuse to explain why. You are entitled to know the reason for your loss of liberty. 3. THE POLICE CANNOT DETAIN YOU INDEFINITELY. Article 14(3) provides that a person arrested or detained on reasonable suspicion of having committed or being about to commit a criminal offence, and who is not released, must be brought before a court within 48 hours. The Attorney-General’s directive emphasises that the clock begins when your liberty is first restrained. Not when the police eventually record your arrest. The 48-hour rule is a constitutional command, not a favour from the police. 4. BAIL IS FREE! Yes. Bail is free! The directive expressly prohibits officers from demanding money, gifts or favours as a condition for granting bail. Bail conditions must be lawful and reasonable. And an officer cannot demand payment merely because a suspect or family member wants the suspect released. Nobody should have to buy their constitutional liberty from a police officer. 5. YOU CANNOT BE TORTURED OR FORCED TO CONFESS. Article 15 protects human dignity. The law prohibits torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. Investigators must not beat, threaten, humiliate or intimidate suspects into making statements. The Evidence Act also regulates the admissibility of confessions and requires safeguards against involuntary statements. A confession extracted through unlawful coercion is not justice. 6. YOU HAVE A RIGHT TO LEGAL ASSISTANCE. You have the right to consult a lawyer of your choice. The Attorney-General’s directive reinforces safeguards governing the taking of statements, including the use of independent witnesses where required by law. If you do not understand the language being used, appropriate interpretation must be provided. And you must not be compelled to sign a statement you do not understand or agree with. Do not sign a statement merely because an investigator demands it. 7. THE POLICE CANNOT SEARCH OR SEIZE PROPERTY HOWEVER THEY PLEASE. Searches must comply with the Constitution and applicable laws. Where a warrant is required, investigators must obtain one. Seized items must be properly recorded, labelled and preserved. Investigators cannot simply take your property and treat it as their personal possession. The same principle applies to electronic devices, communications and digital evidence. The power to investigate is not a licence to disregard privacy and property rights. 8. YOUR BANK ACCOUNT CANNOT BE FROZEN ARBITRARILY. Investigators must have lawful authority to freeze bank accounts or seize assets. Where the applicable statute requires judicial confirmation, that requirement must be observed. The directive also prohibits using asset-freezing powers to coerce suspects into settlements. An allegation against you does not automatically give an investigator unlimited control over your property. 9. BEING ARRESTED DOES NOT MAKE YOU GUILTY. Article 19(2)(c) of the Constitution guarantees the presumption of innocence until guilt is proved or admitted. The directive prohibits investigators from parading suspects before the media or presenting them publicly as guilty before trial. An arrest is not a conviction. A police accusation is not a judicial finding. The dignity of suspects must be respected, however serious the allegations against them. 10. OFFICERS WHO VIOLATE YOUR RIGHTS CAN BE HELD ACCOUNTABLE. This is one of the most significant features of the Attorney-General’s directive. Investigating agencies must maintain proper records, report detention beyond 48 hours, document allegations of ill-treatment and submit quarterly compliance reports. Officers who disregard the law may face disciplinary action, civil liability or criminal prosecution. Article 14(5) also provides a right to compensation for unlawful arrest, restriction or detention. The law does not place investigating officers above accountability. SO, WHAT HAS THE ATTORNEY-GENERAL CHANGED? The Attorney-General has not rewritten the Constitution. These protections already exist. What he has done is to consolidate them into a comprehensive set of operational instructions, demand proper documentation, strengthen prosecutorial supervision and establish reporting and accountability mechanisms. And he deserves commendation. His earlier decision to publicly explain his reasons for entering a nolle prosequi , despite not being expressly required by the Constitution to provide those reasons, and his efforts to improve access to lawyers at police stations, reflect a welcome emphasis on accountability and fairness in criminal justice. But the real test begins now. Will these instructions be obeyed at police stations across Ghana? Will officers who unlawfully detain suspects face consequences? Will bail truly remain free? Will the intimidation, humiliation and extortion stop? May this directive signal the real RESET – the end of the too-familiar abuses. And remember: knowing your rights does not entitle you to obstruct a lawful investigation. Cooperate with lawful processes, seek legal assistance where necessary and challenge abuses through lawful means. The law protects the innocent, guarantees fair treatment to suspects and demands accountability from investigators. THE LAW – It is your legal light, it is your help law. Join me on my weekly legal clinic THE LAW show on the JoyNews Channel every Sunday @ 2:00 PM.

items.title: Cross-border real-time VAT to generate at least GH¢2.5bn in first year, GRA projects
items.description: The full implementation of the real-time Value Added Tax (VAT) system will begin in January next year, with the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) expecting to generate more than GH¢2.5 billion for the country in its first year. According to the Commissioner-General of the Ghana Revenue Authority, Anthony Sarpong, the deployment forms part of measures to close the revenue gap and improve the efficiency of VAT collection. He was speaking at the KPMG Post-Budget Forum in Accra. The 2027 Budget, beyond its focus on the new economy, is expected to address major concerns around employment and domestic revenue mobilisation. According to a pre-budget survey conducted by auditing firm KPMG and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), more businesses require adequate information on tax reforms ahead of their implementation. Speaking at the post-budget forum, Commissioner-General of the Ghana Revenue Authority, Anthony Sarpong, disclosed that the real-time VAT system on cross-border trade would help address revenue gaps in tax collection, with more than GH¢2.5 billion expected to be generated in the first year of implementation. “Based on our preliminary assessment, we are expecting not less than 2.5 billion cedis from the first year of implementation on the real VAT because we have identified more businesses that will be coming on board. We’re also anticipating an increase in the revenue because now we take it from the point of payment. So therefore, we believe that this can give us more visibility in terms of VAT and help close the revenue gap in our tax administration,” he explained. Country Managing Partner of KPMG Ghana, Andy Akoto, highlighted some key policy measures in the 2027 Budget and called for greater support to ensure its implementation. The Country Director of the United Nations Development Programme, Niloy Banerjee, also used the platform to make a case for more citizens to take advantage of the policies outlined in the Budget. This year’s forum was held under the theme, “The New Economy, New Ghana, Jobs and Prosperity”.

items.title: 24-hour economy job claims need evidence for independent verification – Bokpin
items.description: Economist and Professor at the University of Ghana Business School, Professor Godfred Bokpin, has urged the government to provide verifiable data to support its claims of jobs created under the 24-hour economy programme. He says the 24-hour Economy Secretariat must publish details of the companies employing workers, the number of people engaged and the locations of the jobs to enable independent verification. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story on Thursday, November 19, Professor Bokpin said employment figures announced by the government must be supported by evidence, particularly as some of the jobs appear to be temporary, part-time or potentially underemployment. He suggested that the figures could be cross-checked against data from the National Identification Authority (NIA), particularly the number of people paying Pay-As-You-Earn (PAYE) income tax, as well as records of contributions to the Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT). “When they say they have created employment under the 24-hour economy, I think they have to provide the numbers, the companies, how many people have been employed. There are ways of checking that,” he said. Professor Bokpin, however, urged the public to exercise patience, noting that translating campaign promises into tangible results within the first two years of an administration was always going to be challenging. He said the government had also missed an opportunity to use the construction industry as an early driver of employment under the policy. According to him, the sector offers a relatively accessible avenue for expanding employment through additional work shifts, particularly under the government’s Big Push infrastructure programme. He argued that “delays in creating an enabling business environment have made it difficult for private-sector companies to expand operations and employ more workers.” Professor Bokpin further observed that the government’s initial strategy of restoring macroeconomic stability through expenditure cuts, tight monetary policy and liquidity controls could constrain job creation in the short term. He explained that the measures, while aimed at stabilising the economy and reducing inflation, come with short-term costs, including potential employment trade-offs. He said the “24-hour economy cannot operate independently of the broader economic environment”, stressing that businesses need favourable conditions to expand and create sustainable employment.

items.title: President, PM agree on resolving 'all matters' through dialogue amid rising political temperatures
items.description: President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif have decided that all matters will be resolved through dialogue, the Presidency said on Thursday after the two leaders met in Islamabad. The meeting follows recent hard-hitting remarks by President Zardari’s son, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, who questioned past decisions and actions taken by the ruling coalition — steered by PML-N and supported by PPP. In a statement, the Presidency said the “current situation” was discussed in Thursday’s meeting. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, whom Bilawal made pointed remarks about, was also present at the huddle. The “current political situation was reviewed in detail”, while the Middle East conflict also came under discussion. It was decided that the leadership will “sit down together on all matters and resolve them through consultation”, the Presidency said. “The previous constitutional amendments were passed through mutual consultation among all allied parties,” the statement from President Zardari’s office said. The recent friction between coalition partners PML-N and PPP comes amid a debate over the creation of new administrative units, which was sparked by Naqvi in July when he called for a “reset” in governance. The PPP has consistently opposed carving out new provinces in Sindh, which it rules. The party has consistently invoked a unanimous resolution passed by the Sindh Assembly opposing the province’s division, although President Zardari has not commented on the matter publicly. In his remarks on Tuesday, Bilawal voiced his strong opposition to a referendum on creating new provinces, questioning the “intent” behind it, and claimed his party lawmakers were facing “pressure” but would not succumb to it. His speech drew a strong reaction from leaders of the PML-N, as well as the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) — another coalition ally. Such decisions won’t be made without consensus: PML-N Following the high-level huddle, a federal minister from the PML-N affirmed that any key decisions will be taken with consensus — as decided in the meeting. Speaking on Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath’, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry said : “A matter about the people will be decided in a democratic manner, and you cannot exclude parties in that. These are major parties; you cannot even exclude minor parties. Moreover, you cannot make such big decisions without consensus, neither they will be.” Asked if there were efforts underway for reducing tensions between the two allies, Chaudhry said, “This is the appropriate way and this is what mature political parties do.” He remarked that Bilawal, being a young politician, made a passionate speech, but then later he “kept trying to explain it”. “Today, his father, the president, he has always wanted to take things forward with dialogue,” the minister noted. Asked if he had also been issued directives by PM Shehbaz to adopt a softer tone, Chaudhry stressed the “shared responsibility” of the two parties, noting that all constitutional roles in the incumbent government come into existence because of this coalition. He contended that although the PML-N gave a response, it did not say anything “emotional” as Bilawal did. The minister further wondered why the PPP chairman did not show tolerance for others’ point of view, while he urged others to do the same for his opinions. “Who said this was happening or was about to happen?” Chaudhry said, referring to the creation of provinces, adding that “each and every small action” has always been done with consultation. The state minister explained there was a committee for matters regarding lawmaking where “each and every thing” is presented to all coalition partners before it is tabled in the Parliament, including the constitutional amendments. Asked if the process of new provinces will continue despite PPP’s objection to Sindh’s division, Chaudhry emphasised that the discussion pertained to the entire country, not just any one province. “Secondly, it will be taken forward in a political, democratic and constitutional manner, and there is consensus on this since Day One,” he declared, asserting that even minor decisions since the coalition came to power in 2022 were made after comprehensive consultations. “We have the courage to hear criticism and we will keep doing so,” the PML-N leader added, terming today’s statement by the Presidency as “the best”. Asked about the PML-N’s point of view, Chaudhry stressed that his PML-N was the entire country’s party, not just of Punjab. He said the PML-N’s stance was that the discussion on governance should take place across the entire country. “You cannot clap with one hand,” he said when asked about Bilawal’s suggestion on returning reserved seats , and recalled PTI’s actions, including May 9 riots, protests in the capital, and mass resignations from assemblies. On engagement with PTI regarding governor’s rule in KP, Chaudhry said the government already clarified it has no political aims behind the measures. “If they agree, then why would we object, but these things cannot be settled in a day or immediately.” What has Bilawal said? Despite months having passed since the debate began, Bilawal claimed that no one from the government had brought up the matter with him or President Zardari, even though some federal ministers have voiced their support for more provinces. His remarks followed the Nov 14 meeting between President Zardari and PM Shehbaz. According to official sources, the two reached an understanding on sticking to the constitutional process for any new provinces. Speaking at a ‘Meet the Press’ event in Karachi, the Bhutto scion expressed the fear that any “forced” attempt to carve up Sindh into new provinces would lead to bloodshed. He also voiced his strong opposition to a referendum on creating new provinces — as initially suggested by Naqvi and endorsed by Information Minister Attaullah Tarar in response to Bilawal’s speech. Bilawal even questioned whether the judiciary had the public’s confidence, particularly in the wake of the 27th Amendment, which he had strongly advocated for at the time of its passage just a year ago. He said that the 27th Amendment was passed with a “ brute majority ” rather than a mutual consensus. However, in a later interview, Bilawal clarified that he was not “disowning” the amendment, but rather advocating for greater consensus on such key legislation. As he called for a “political and democratic reset” to meet the growing economic challenges, the PPP chairman suggested some steps the government could take to restore the opposition’s confidence so the Parliament could function properly.

items.title: Présidentielle en France : l’Arcom soumet les youtubeurs au respect du «pluralisme politique»
items.description: « Lors des elections presidentielles 2027, les createurs de contenus doivent respecter les regles de pluralisme politique dans le traitement de l'actualite electorale », a annonce ce 19 novembre par voie de communique le gendarme de l'audiovisuel francais, l'Arcom. « Les createurs de contenus doivent respecter l'equite, puis l'egalite, entre les candidats, ainsi que l'obligation de mesure et d'honnetete dans le traitement de l'actualite electorale », est-il precise. Des regles qui jusqu'alors s'imposaient aux chaînes de television ainsi qu'aux radios. « Il y a un phenomene nouveau, il est la et il est massif », a justifie le president de l'Arcom, Martin Ajdari, lors d'une conference de presse, selon des propos rapportes par l'AFP, concernant cette mesure qui vise uniquement les contenus video. « Les podcasts audio ne sont pas concernes », a precise Ajdari. « Cette question se pose concretement pour des createurs dont les audiences depassent celles de chaînes » de television, a defendu cet ex-directeur general delegue de Radio France et directeur de cabinet des ministres de la Culture Aurelie Filippetti et Fleur Pellerin, en faisant le parallele avec le podcasteur americain Joe Rogan que des medias francais depeignent comme un « fervent soutien de Trump ». L'« influence » des createurs de contenus concernes sera appreciee en fonction de trois criteres : le « contenu », l'« impact » et la « regularite ». Une chaîne « consacree exclusivement au jeu video, a la cuisine ou au sport, sans incursion reguliere dans le debat public » ne remplit pas ces criteres, a notamment illustre l'Arcom dans son communique. En revanche, elle sera concernee « si elle touche un public significatif a l'image d'un media audiovisuel et si elle a une influence sur une partie de la population ». En cas de manquements, « on peut prendre des sanctions » envers ces createurs de contenus consideres comme des editeurs, au meme titre qu'une chaîne de television ou qu'une radio, a averti Martin Ajdari. Lorsqu'elle estime qu'il y a eu un manquement, l'Arcom peut adresser un rappel, puis une mise en garde et enfin une mise en demeure, avant de passer a des sanctions financieres.

items.title: Formation universitaire : El Midaoui appelle les entreprises à exprimer leurs besoins
items.description: Alors que plus de 73 % des entreprises interrogées estiment que les diplômés ne sont pas suffisamment préparés aux exigences du marché du travail, la question de l'adéquation entre formation universitaire et besoins économiques reste un défi pour l'enseignement supérieur marocain. Lors de la conférence de presse tenue jeudi 19 novembre à l'issue du Conseil de gouvernement, le ministre de l'Enseignement supérieur, de la recherche scientifique et de l'innovation, Azzedine El Midaoui, a défendu une approche fondée sur une implication accrue des entreprises dans la conception des formations, tout en plaidant pour une université capable de préparer les étudiants aux mutations économiques, technologiques et professionnelles. Selon les conclusions d’un récent rapport du Conseil supérieur de l’éducation, de la formation et de la recherche scientifique consacré au bilan de la dernière décennie de réformes éducatives, il y a un paradoxe entre le nombre important de publications scientifiques et les difficultés d’adéquation entre les compétences des diplômés et les attentes des entreprises. © Mounir Mehimdate En réponse à cette question, El Midaoui a rappelé que le taux d’insertion professionnelle constituait le principal indicateur de la qualité d’une formation et de la réussite d’une réforme pédagogique. Il a toutefois tenu à nuancer cette approche, estimant que la mission de l’université ne pouvait être réduite à la seule préparation à l’emploi. L’enseignement, a-t-il rappelé, est aussi un espace de production et de transmission des connaissances. Le ministre a surtout souligné que l’insertion professionnelle dépendait en premier lieu du niveau de croissance économique. Même un diplômé doté de compétences importantes et d’un fort potentiel ne peut être recruté si les entreprises privées ne souhaitent pas embaucher ou n’en ont pas les moyens. Pour illustrer son propos, il a évoqué l’attractivité des compétences marocaines auprès des entreprises internationales. Il s’est notamment interrogé sur les raisons pour lesquelles des sociétés étrangères viennent recruter des ingénieurs, des médecins et des diplômés de master marocains, parfois pour les faire travailler à l’étranger. Il a également cité le cas de plusieurs institutions internationales implantées au Maroc, qui emploieraient près de 100 % de leurs cadres parmi les diplômés des universités marocaines, qu’elles soient publiques, privées ou à but non lucratif. Cette reconnaissance des compétences nationales ne dispense cependant pas les universités de revoir régulièrement leurs programmes, a-t-il précisé. L’objectif est de tenir compte des mutations économiques, industrielles et technologiques, ainsi que de l’évolution des besoins du marché du travail. Les entreprises appelées à participer à l’élaboration des formations Sur ce volet, le ministre a mis en avant les dispositions de la loi n° 24-59 et les décisions relatives aux cahiers des normes pédagogiques, qui accordent, selon lui, une place accrue aux partenaires socio-économiques. Ces derniers ne sont plus seulement appelés à intervenir dans l’insertion professionnelle des diplômés, mais également à participer aux enseignements et à l’élaboration des programmes de formation. « Dites-nous ce dont vous avez besoin », a-t-il lancé à l’adresse des entreprises, affirmant que les universités étaient disposées à travailler avec elles pour définir précisément les profils recherchés et adapter les formations à leurs attentes. Il a rappelé qu’il formulait déjà cet appel lorsqu’il présidait une université. Le ministre a, dans ce sens, cité les contrats conclus entre l’État et les universités marocaines dans trois secteurs prioritaires : la santé, la digitalisation et l’éducation, notamment pour la formation des enseignants destinés à rejoindre le secteur de l’Éducation nationale. Selon lui, les engagements pris dans le cadre de ces trois chantiers ont été entièrement réalisés, voire dépassés. Certaines formations ont ainsi dépassé les objectifs fixés de 100 %, tandis que d’autres ont atteint un taux de réalisation de 120 %. Des résultats qu’il a présentés comme la preuve de la capacité des universités à répondre aux besoins exprimés par leurs partenaires institutionnels. El Midaoui a également assuré que les nouveaux textes législatifs et réglementaires permettraient d’intégrer davantage ces partenaires dans les structures universitaires. Le ministère se dit prêt à examiner leurs demandes, jusque dans leurs aspects les plus précis, et à adapter les formations aux profils attendus. Former des esprits capables de s’adapter aux mutations Au-delà de l’adéquation immédiate entre les diplômes et les emplois disponibles, le ministre a défendu une conception plus large de la formation universitaire. Selon lui, l’enjeu n’est pas seulement de produire des spécialistes dans un domaine donné, mais de former des diplômés capables de s’adapter à des environnements professionnels en constante évolution. Il a pris l’exemple d’un ingénieur en génie électrique qui, après quelques années en entreprise, peut être amené à exercer des fonctions différentes de celles pour lesquelles il avait initialement été formé. La valeur de la formation universitaire réside précisément, selon lui, dans les outils intellectuels et les compétences transversales qui lui permettent de s’adapter à ces changements. « La première chose que nous devons préparer, c’est un esprit bien formé, une tête bien faite », a-t-il insisté. Une formation solide doit, à ses yeux, permettre aux diplômés de s’insérer rapidement dans différents secteurs, sans être enfermés dans une spécialisation trop étroite. Cette approche doit néanmoins rester ancrée dans les constantes nationales, la culture et l’identité marocaines, a-t-il ajouté. Le défi consiste à concilier cet ancrage avec la capacité à accompagner les transformations économiques, industrielles et technologiques, dont le rythme s’accélère. Reconnaissant que des efforts supplémentaires restent nécessaires, le ministre a appelé à intensifier le travail de réforme afin d’accompagner les grands chantiers engagés par le Maroc sous l’impulsion du roi Mohammed VI. Il a rappelé que les universités constituaient, selon lui, le moteur de cette dynamique, puisqu’elles sont chargées de former les compétences nécessaires à sa réalisation. Enfin, il a insisté sur la nécessité de mieux prendre en compte les besoins des territoires, à l’échelle régionale comme locale, tout en développant une vision prospective des métiers à l’échelle internationale. Avec l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle et la transformation des activités professionnelles, les métiers tendent de moins en moins à être circonscrits à un marché local. Pour El Midaoui, l’université doit donc anticiper ces évolutions et préparer des diplômés capables d’évoluer dans des environnements professionnels variés. Une manière de rappeler que, si l’insertion professionnelle demeure un indicateur essentiel de la qualité des formations, la capacité d’adaptation des diplômés constitue aussi l’un des objectifs centraux de l’enseignement supérieur. The post Formation universitaire : El Midaoui appelle les entreprises à exprimer leurs besoins appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Samson’s Take: AG Ayine’s Directive: May this signal the end of the familiar abuses!
items.description: Today, Thursday, 19 th November, 2026, is one of those days when I write and publish Samson’s Take ahead of Saturday. For years, we have complained about arbitrary arrests, unlawful detentions, coerced confessions, the commercialisation of bail, the humiliation of suspects and the weaponisation of criminal investigations. We have watched people arrested over civil disputes, detained beyond the constitutional 48 hours, paraded before television cameras as criminals and subjected to investigations that sometimes appear designed more to punish than to establish the truth. These abuses have become far too familiar. And that is why Attorney-General and Minister for Justice, Dr Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, deserves commendation for his latest intervention. First, he took the unusual and commendable step of publicly explaining his reasons for entering a nolle prosequi , discontinuing criminal proceedings, although the Constitution does not expressly oblige him to provide those reasons. He has also championed improved access to lawyers at police stations, recognising that the right to legal representation must mean something at the earliest and often most vulnerable stage of the criminal process. Now comes his comprehensive Directive on Constitutional and Legal Compliance in the Conduct of Criminal Investigations , dated November 2, 2026. And what a necessary intervention! The directive addresses virtually every major abuse that has undermined public confidence in criminal investigations. No arbitrary arrests! An arrest must rest on lawful grounds. Investigators must not use arrest or detention to intimidate citizens, settle personal scores, recover debts or enforce contracts. No unlawful detention! The Constitution requires suspects arrested on reasonable suspicion and not released to be brought before a court within 48 hours. And the Attorney-General makes an important point: that period runs from the moment liberty is first restrained, not from the time an officer conveniently enters the arrest in a diary. No more manipulating the clock! No torture! No threats! No coerced confessions! Suspects must be treated with dignity. They must understand the allegations against them and enjoy the safeguards the law provides when statements are taken. Investigators must not manufacture evidence or intimidate suspects into confessing to offences. And bail is free! The directive expressly prohibits demanding payment, gifts or favours as conditions for bail. How many Ghanaians have suffered because an officer treated the grant of bail as an opportunity to make money? How many families have been compelled to pay simply to secure the liberty of relatives who ought to have been released without payment? May this directive signal the end of that disgraceful practice! The Attorney-General also confronts another disturbing abuse: the unlawful freezing and seizure of people’s assets. Bank accounts and property cannot be frozen merely because an investigator considers it convenient. The law must authorise the action, and the necessary judicial processes must be respected. Asset-freezing powers must not become instruments for intimidation or coercing settlements. And what about the familiar spectacle of suspects being paraded before cameras? People arrested on suspicion are sometimes presented to the public as though their guilt has already been established. The directive says no! An arrest is not a conviction. An allegation is not proof. And a suspect does not lose the presumption of innocence merely because the police have invited the media! There are equally important provisions on searches, digital surveillance, protection of children, victims and witnesses, disclosure of evidence and prosecutorial supervision. But perhaps the most consequential aspect of this directive is its insistence on accountability . Every material investigative decision must be recorded, reasoned and open to review. Investigating agencies must maintain records, report instances of detention beyond 48 hours, document allegations of ill-treatment and submit quarterly compliance reports. And officers who violate the law may face disciplinary action, civil liability or criminal prosecution. That is how constitutional guarantees begin to acquire practical meaning! Of course, the Attorney-General has not invented these rights. They already exist in our Constitution and statutes. What he has done is to bring them together, confront recurring violations directly and demand that those entrusted with enforcing the law themselves obey it. And that deserves praise. But there is a caution. Ghana does not suffer primarily from a shortage of constitutional guarantees. We suffer from their repeated violation, often without consequences. We have seen too many directives issued, too many assurances given and too many abuses repeated. The real test will therefore not be how widely this document circulates. It will be what happens when the next suspect is unlawfully detained. When the next investigator demands money for bail. When the next officer uses arrest to recover a debt. When the next suspect is tortured, humiliated or paraded before cameras. Will there be consequences? Will supervisors enforce these instructions? Will the Attorney-General demand the promised reports? Will officers who violate the law be held personally accountable? And will the political authorities respect these standards even when investigations involve their opponents? Because the rule of law must protect everyone – the powerful and the powerless, the popular and the unpopular, the political friend and the political adversary. Constitutional rights are not privileges to be dispensed according to political convenience. Attorney-General Ayine has taken an important step in the right direction. He deserves encouragement and support, just as he must be held to the standards he has now set. For the ordinary Ghanaian, the promise is simple: that an encounter with law enforcement should not mean the suspension of one’s constitutional rights. That the police station should not become a place of extortion. That investigation should be a search for truth, not an instrument of punishment. And that the authority of the state must always be exercised according to law. May this directive not become another beautiful document gathering dust on official shelves. May it signal the end of the too-familiar abuses that have made criminal investigations a source of fear rather than confidence. And may the Attorney-General be remembered not merely for issuing this directive, but for ensuring that it was obeyed! And that is My Take.

items.title: BoG blacklists Cedi Trust, SikaPadi, 17 other loan apps over privacy violations
items.description: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has issued a public alert warning citizens against engaging with 19 digital credit applications operating in the country without the requisite licence or authorisation. In a notice signed by the Secretary of the Bank, Aimee Vyda Quashie, the central bank stated that the operations of these entities constitute significant violations of customer data privacy, consumer protection, and established regulatory standards. The directive was issued in collaboration with the CyberSecurity Authority and directly contravenes the Directive for Digital Credit Service Providers in Ghana, issued in September 2025. The Bank named the following mobile loan applications as operating without a licence: Cedi Trust, CediCredit, Codo, Easy Moni, EasyRate Loan, Focus Loan, Gaga Credit, Hold Cash, Hope Funds, Mondi Money, Monifi, Pulse Cash, Quick Loan – Easy Cash Loan, Score Cash, Sika Bosea, Sika Prime, SikaPadi, SmoothCash, and SoarCredit. The central bank has urged the general public to refrain from doing business with these unlicensed providers. It advised prospective borrowers to verify the licensing status of any digital credit provider by checking the Bank of Ghana’s official website before using their services. Furthermore, the Bank has cautioned banks, Specialised Deposit-Taking Institutions, and Payment Service Providers against facilitating or processing transactions on behalf of these unlicensed loan providers. The Bank of Ghana emphasised that it will continue to collaborate with relevant state institutions to identify, investigate, and take appropriate enforcement action against such entities to safeguard consumers and uphold the integrity and stability of the financial sector. Members of the public who become aware of the activities of unlicensed loan providers have been encouraged to report them to the Fintech and Innovation Department of the Bank of Ghana. Reports can be made via telephone or text on shortcode 292, or through email at fintech@bog.gov.gh, digitalcredit@bog.gov.gh, and report@csa.gov.gh.
